summary.text: Emerald is a gemstone variety of the mineral beryl, turned green by trace amounts of chromium or sometimes vanadium.
Most emeralds are full of inclusions and fissures, so almost all are treated with oil to improve how clear they look.
Colour matters most in grading, and the top stones are a vivid, well-saturated green in a medium-dark tone.

facts.label: Nickname for inclusions
facts.value: Jardin, French for garden, for their mossy look

facts.label: Signature cut
facts.value: Rectangular emerald cut with faceted top edge

items.prompt: A pale green gem is chemically the same mineral as emerald but very light in tone. What would a gemologist call it?

options.label: A light emerald
A green sapphire
Green beryl
A flawed emerald

items.explain: Only medium to dark gems count as emeralds; light-toned ones go by the species name green beryl.

items.prompt: Emerald scores 7.5–8 on the Mohs hardness scale, yet jewellers warn it can crack if knocked. Why?

options.label: Its many inclusions give it poor toughness
Its chromium makes the crystal brittle
Its oil treatment softens the stone
Hardness numbers above 7 mean fragility

items.explain: Most emeralds have many inclusions, so even though beryl is fairly hard, their toughness is classified as poor.

items.prompt: Two emeralds look equally good, but one was oil-treated and the other was not. How do their values usually compare?

options.label: Both are worth the same, since oiling is accepted
The untreated stone is worth much more
The oiled stone is worth more because it is clearer
The oiled stone cannot legally be sold

items.explain: Oiling is traditional and widely accepted, but oil-treated emeralds are worth much less than untreated ones of similar quality.

items.prompt: A diamond grader uses a 10× loupe to judge clarity. How is an emerald's clarity judged instead?

options.label: Under a stronger 30× microscope
By weighing it in water
By shining ultraviolet light through it
With the naked eye

items.explain: Emeralds are graded by eye, so one with no inclusions visible to normal sight counts as flawless.

items.prompt: A seller offers emeralds that were soaked in green-tinted oil to deepen their colour. How does the gem trade view this?

options.label: It is the standard, accepted treatment
It is accepted if the oil is cedar-based
It is not acceptable
It raises the stone's grade by one step

items.explain: Clear oils that fill cracks are accepted, but treatments such as green-tinted oil are not acceptable in the trade.

items.prompt: Why are emeralds often cut as smooth domed cabochons rather than in faceted shapes?

options.label: Facets would make them too bright to look at
The stones are not uniform inside
They are too hard for faceting tools
Domes are required by trade law

items.explain: Emeralds' relative non-uniformity encourages cutting them as cabochons instead of faceted shapes.
